What it means: Someone is named responsible for cybersecurity risk, and everyone knows who
Why it maps: All three require named, written ownership of security and risk. PM-2 names a security program lead, PS-9 puts security duties in position descriptions, and SOC 2 CC1.3 asks for defined authorities and reporting lines. The firm has only an informal COO contact.

What it means: The company has a written policy for managing cybersecurity risk
Why it maps: Each 800-53 family starts with a '-1' policy control. Your three Phase 5 policies line up with AC-1 (access control), IR-1 (incident response), and PL-4 Rules of Behavior (acceptable use). ISO 5.10 is the acceptable use control.

What it means: Vendors must meet security requirements, and those requirements are written into contracts
Why it maps: Security requirements belong in supplier contracts (SA-4, ISO 5.20) and suppliers should be assessed (SR-6, CC9.2). The help desk contract has no security terms and the processor attestation is missing.

What it means: The company keeps a list of its software, services, and systems
Why it maps: Asset inventory. CM-8 is the system component inventory, and SOC 2 CC6.1 includes identifying and managing the inventory of information assets. Your Assets tab satisfies this.

What it means: Assets are ranked by how sensitive and how important they are
Why it maps: Classification and criticality. RA-2 is security categorization and RA-9 is criticality analysis, matching your classification column and 1-5 criticality score.

What it means: Weaknesses in systems are found and written down
Why it maps: Vulnerability identification. RA-5 is vulnerability monitoring and scanning, and SOC 2 CC7.1 covers detecting newly discovered vulnerabilities. No routine scanning is the gap.

What it means: Threats, weaknesses, likelihood, and impact are used to rank risks
Why it maps: Risk assessment itself. RA-3 is the risk assessment control and CC3.2 asks the entity to identify and analyze risk. In ISO this sits in the main clauses, not Annex A. Your 5x5 Risk Register satisfies this.

What it means: Each person, service, and device has its own managed identity and credentials
Why it maps: Unique identities. IA-2 requires each user to be uniquely identified, so the shared clearinghouse login and shared backup console password both fail it.

What it means: Users, services, and hardware prove who they are before getting access
Why it maps: MFA. IA-2(1) is MFA for privileged accounts and IA-2(2) is MFA for non-privileged accounts, so the firm meets IA-2(1) (2 admins) but not IA-2(2) (50 staff). AC-17 and CC6.6 cover remote access, which is the password-only VPN.

What it means: Access is defined in a policy, limited to what each job needs, and reviewed
Why it maps: Least privilege and access reviews. AC-6 is least privilege, AC-2 includes periodic account review, PS-4 and PS-5 cover leavers and movers, and CC6.2 and CC6.3 cover provisioning, modifying, and removing access.

What it means: Physical access to offices, devices, and paper records is controlled
Why it maps: Physical access, including paper. In 800-53, 'media' includes paper, so unlocked cabinets fall under MP-4 (media storage) and the monthly shred bin under MP-6 (sanitization). ISO 7.7 is clear desk.

What it means: Staff get security awareness and training that fits their jobs
Why it maps: Awareness training. AT-2(1) is practical exercises such as phishing simulations and AT-2(3) is social engineering awareness. Both match GAP-02.

What it means: People in specialized roles get training that fits their risks
Why it maps: Role-based training. AT-3 covers training for specialized roles, here payroll staff who must spot fake bank-detail change requests.

What it means: Stored data is protected, for example by encryption
Why it maps: Encryption at rest. AC-19(5) is full-device encryption for mobile devices like laptops, SC-28(1) is cryptographic protection of stored data, and SC-12 covers the recovery keys in GAP-11.

What it means: Backups are created, protected, and tested
Why it maps: Backups. CP-9 is system backup and CP-9(1) is testing backups for reliability and integrity. SOC 2 A1.x applies only if the Availability category is in scope.

What it means: Systems are set up in a standard, managed way
Why it maps: Standard configurations. CM-2 is the baseline configuration, CM-6 the settings, and CM-7 least functionality. CC7.1 asks for defined configuration standards, and central device management (GAP-04) is how you enforce them.

What it means: Software is kept up to date and old software is retired
Why it maps: Patching. SI-2 is flaw remediation and SA-22 covers unsupported software. SOC 2 treats patches as changes under CC8.1.

What it means: Networks are protected from unauthorized access
Why it maps: Network protection. SC-7 is boundary protection (the default-config firewall), AC-17 is remote access (the VPN), and CC6.6 covers access from outside system boundaries.

What it means: Staff activity and technology use are watched for signs of trouble
Why it maps: Monitoring. AU-6 is audit record review, SI-4 is system monitoring, and AC-2(12) is monitoring accounts for unusual use. Nobody reviews Microsoft 365 sign-in logs.

What it means: Suspicious events are analyzed to understand what is happening
Why it maps: Event analysis. CC7.3 and ISO 5.25 both ask the organization to evaluate events and decide whether they are incidents. There is no process for that today.

What it means: The incident response plan is carried out once an incident is declared
Why it maps: Incident response. IR-8 is the written plan, IR-4 is incident handling, and IR-3 is testing it, which matches the practice drill in GAP-15.

What it means: The right people inside and outside the company are told about incidents
Why it maps: Notification. IR-6 is incident reporting and CC2.3 covers communicating with external parties. As a HIPAA business associate, the firm must also notify each covered entity of a breach under 45 CFR 164.410.

What it means: Recovery steps are carried out once recovery starts
Why it maps: Recovery. CP-2 is the contingency plan and CP-10 is system recovery. CC7.5 asks for recovery activities after incidents. GAP-09's runbook is the fix.

What it means: Backups are checked for integrity before they are used to restore
Why it maps: Backup integrity before restore. CP-9(1) tests backups for integrity, CP-4 tests the contingency plan, and A1.3 includes testing the integrity and completeness of backup data.
